gaps.fact: The Court's red Producers cells for vodka (eight names), rum (seven) and gin (six). No chapter, stem or service table names a vodka, rum or gin producer; the serviceRef spirits table says by design that it states no producer.
The Court's red Producers cells for tequila (eight names) and mezcal (three: Bozal, Del Maguey, Wahaka). None is named anywhere in the Codex.

The Court's red Producers cells for bourbon (six), Tennessee (two), Canadian (three), Irish (four), Scotch by region (Highland and Speyside four, Lowland two, Islay five) and blended Scotch (seven). None is named anywhere in the Codex.
The Court's red Producers cells for Cognac (four houses) and Armagnac (Larressingle, Delord, Montal). None is named anywhere in the Codex.

Most of the Court's liqueur list is never taught by name: Pimm's, Crème de Menthe and Frangelico (herb and nut); Anisette and Galliano (anise); Southern Comfort (peach); Baileys (cream); Drambuie, Glayva and Irish Mist (whiskey); St. Germain (elderflower), Canton (ginger), Kahlúa and Tia Maria (coffee). Chartreuse is keyed (i-rkjnuhsz), amaretto and sambuca appear as distractors, and Cointreau, Grand Marnier, triple sec and Bénédictine sit in the serviceRef tables only.
Rum styles: Light, Dark, Aged, Spiced. Named only in the serviceRef spirits row and in the explanation of s-qmqmc2tu; no chapter fact or stem in either bank.

Tequila: Jalisco; Mezcal: Oaxaca. Both are in the Village chapter and the serviceRef spirits rows, but no stem keys either state (Jalisco appears only in explanations, of i-d8mr9onv as tequila's home and of c-6g4e3ft1 as raicilla's; Oaxaca in no stem or explanation).

Mezcal's age classes, Blanco (most common), Reposado, Añejo. Only the serviceRef spirits row gives them (as Joven, Reposado and Añejo); the bank asks mezcal's production classes (c-ch423mwo) but never its ageing.

Canadian whisky: at least 3 years in oak, from corn, wheat, rye or barley, typically column distilled (the Court's Raw Material and Type of distillation cells as well). Only the serviceRef spirits row says Canadian whisky is aged three years and need not be made of rye; no chapter fact or stem teaches Canadian whisky at all.
Scotch is distilled twice in pot stills, but the Lowlands traditionally three times. The Lowland triple distillation is never taught; c-uhl3ec8a gives the third pass to Irish whiskey alone.
Tennessee whiskey: at least 51 per cent corn, as bourbon. Implied only by the serviceRef spirits row (bourbon by recipe); no chapter or stem gives Tennessee's grain.
Calvados: a minimum of 2 years in oak; Armagnac's VS, VSOP and XO steps. Both sit in the serviceRef digestifs rows only; no chapter fact or stem gives a Calvados age or an Armagnac age term.

Eaux de vie de fruits: Framboise (raspberry), Kirsch (cherry), Poire William (pear), French, generally unaged (the Court's Raw Material and Distinct process cells as well). Only the serviceRef digestifs and spirits rows teach them; no chapter fact or stem.
Armagnac's three subregions, Bas Armagnac, Ténarèze and Haut Armagnac. Listed in the Village chapter; no stem asks them (Bas-Armagnac is praised in the explanation of i-jue1wk1u only).

Pomace brandy: Grappa from Italy, Marc from France, generally unaged. The Village chapter states it, but no stem asks what grappa or marc is made from (c-100giccw names Marc de Bourgogne only as the cheese's wash).

courtUpdates.now: The United States added American Single Malt Whisky to its standards of identity: 100 per cent malted barley, mashed, distilled and matured at one United States distillery, distilled at no more than 160 proof, with a Straight American Single Malt at two years or more; published in the Federal Register on 18 December 2024, in force from 19 January 2025, with a transition for bottlings before 19 January 2030. The Court's table prints no American malt style, so the cell stands; this is for our own note.
courtUpdates.source: TTB, Addition of American Single Malt Whisky to the Standards of Identity for Distilled Spirits, Federal Register 89 FR 102726, 18 December 2024; TTB announcement of the final rule

notes: Mapped questions: Régionale 64 (Sake & Spirits, of which 31 are on spirits and liqueurs), Village 54 (Spirits & Cocktails, of which 48 are on spirits, liqueurs and aromatised wines and 6 on cocktails), 118 in all and 79 on spirits; one service question (s-p1q43sq4) adds Calvados Pays d'Auge. The Codex is strong on Cognac, Scotch, bourbon law and agave and pitched above the Court there (the compte, XXO, Blanche Armagnac, Bottled in Bond, Jamaican esters, mezcal classes), but every red Producers cell is a gap: the Court asks for about seventy brand names across vodka, rum, gin, tequila, mezcal, the whiskies and the brandies and the Codex names none, by design in the serviceRef spirits table. Canadian whisky, the Lowland triple distillation, rum styles, mezcal ageing, Calvados and Armagnac age terms and the eaux de vie are the other holes; the last three live only in the service tables. Court cells to read with care in our own copy: Armagnac 'VS/Three Star: 2 years' where the Codex's own digestifs row gives one year in oak, the figure we understand the Armagnac rules to set (to be checked against the interprofession's rules before keying), so an e- question should avoid the VS step or name both figures; 'Ténerèze' is the Court's misspelling of Ténarèze; Amaretto is filed under Apricot (the kernels) while the Codex calls it almond scented, both defensible; 'Hennessey', 'Kettle One', 'Laphroig' and 'Jack Daniels' are the Court's spellings of Hennessy, Ketel One, Laphroaig and Jack Daniel's; the Whisk(e)y raw material row gives Tennessee and bourbon the same 51 per cent corn. Two searches spent: on the tequila standard, which found no confirmed change to the categories or ageing classes since 8.2023 (no update logged), and on the American single malt standard of identity, logged above.
